questions.question:
The readings are stored as a list of integers, one per second. The nightly analysis must finish in a few seconds on the device, and it must report the run lengths exactly.

(a)

Explain, by tracing the loop, what steady_runs returns for the readings [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with the default tolerance of 5.

[3]

(b)

Explain why the developer's claim that the function runs in linear time is unsound. State the property of the input that the claim assumes, and describe the input pattern on which the function performs the greatest number of steps.

[4]

(c)

Construct a Python function that returns exactly the same result as steady_runs but runs in linear time. You may not import any module and you may not use the abs function. A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm, so write the algorithm rather than a demonstration of syntax.

[5]

(d)

A colleague proposes to fix the performance by adding a limit inside the while loop so that it stops after at most 1,000 steps. Evaluate this proposal, using your answers to parts (b) and (c).

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Tracing the loop for readings = [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with tol = 5:

| i | readings[i] | comparisons in the while | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 70 | j = 0, loop does not run | 0 |
| 1 | 72 | $\lvert 72-70 \rvert = 2 \le 5 \rightarrow 1$ | 1 |
| 2 | 71 | $\lvert 71-72 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 71-70 \rvert = 1$ | 2 |
| 3 | 90 | $\lvert 90-71 \rvert = 19 > 5$ | 0 |
| 4 | 89 | $\lvert 89-90 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 89-71 \rvert = 18 > 5$ | 1 |
| 5 | 88 | $1$, then $2$, then $\lvert 88-71 \rvert = 17 > 5$ | 2 |
| 6 | 87 | $1$, then $2$, then $3$, then $\lvert 87-71 \rvert = 16 > 5$ | 3 |

The function returns [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3]. (M1) for tracing the loop as a walk backwards while consecutive differences stay within the tolerance, (A1) for the correct values, (A1) for the list as a whole, including the reset to 0 at index 3 and the growing run at the end.

(b) The claim is unsound because the number of steps the inner loop performs is not a constant — it is the length of the steady run, which is a property of the *data*, not of the code. (M1) The claim assumes that consecutive readings almost always differ by more than the tolerance, so that the loop exits after one or two steps. (A1) That assumption is false for this application: heart rate sampled once a second during steady exercise changes by far less than 5 beats per minute between consecutive samples, so long runs are the normal case and the loop walks back a long way. (A1) The greatest number of steps occurs when every consecutive difference is within tolerance — a constant series, or a slow monotonic drift. For each $i$ the loop then runs all the way back to index 0, giving $0+1+2+\dots+(n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ steps, which is quadratic rather than linear. (A1)

(c)

def steady_runs(readings, tol=5):
    n = len(readings)
    runs = [0] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        step = readings[i] - readings[i - 1]
        if -tol <= step <= tol:
            runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1
    return runs

(M1) for a single pass that keeps no inner loop. (A1) for the observation that makes it work: the steady run ending at i is either empty or it is the run ending at i - 1 extended by exactly one reading, so the answer for i can be read off the answer for i - 1. (A1) for runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1 and (A1) for initialising every entry to 0, which is what makes the run reset after a step larger than the tolerance. (A1) for using no library module and no abs, expressing the tolerance as the two-sided test -tol <= step <= tol.

The work done is $n-1$ comparisons and one assignment per reading, so the time is $O(n)$ and the extra memory is $O(n)$ for the output. A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm; the translation is a for loop over the array indices and the identical recurrence, so the language is irrelevant to the reasoning.

(d) The proposal should be rejected, for three reasons.

First, it does not change the complexity. The inner loop can still run up to 1,000 steps for every reading, so the worst case is still proportional to $1000n$; capping the loop divides the running time by a constant, and a constant factor is not a change of order. (M1) With 86,400 readings a day the uncapped worst case is $86{,}400 \times 86{,}399 / 2 = 3{,}732{,}436{,}800$ inner steps, the capped version still performs up to $86{,}400 \times 1000 = 86{,}400{,}000$, and the linear version performs 86,399. (A1)

Second, and more seriously, the cap makes the result *wrong* precisely where the app matters. A steady run of 1,500 readings would be reported as 1,000, and a run of 4,000 as 1,000; the error is silent, it is always an under-report, and it is concentrated on the longest runs — which are exactly the steady states the app exists to find. (A1)

Third, the trade is unnecessary, because part (c) already gives an exact linear algorithm. Capping the loop trades a correctness guarantee for a constant factor when a change of order was available at the same cost. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question is built around a claim that is easy to believe and easy to falsify: "the inner loop breaks almost immediately, so the function is linear". The claim is not about the code at all; it is about the input. A complexity statement is a statement about *all* inputs, and one input family is enough to destroy it. The family here is a steady recording, and the irony is that steady recordings are exactly what the app is designed to detect. The algorithm is slowest on the data it exists to find.

The mechanism is worth stating in general terms because it recurs everywhere. When a loop's work per iteration depends on the data, the total work is the sum of those per-iteration amounts, and the average tells you nothing about the maximum. Here the per-iteration amount is the run length; if run lengths are bounded by a small constant the total is linear, and if a single run can be as long as the input the total is quadratic. The programmer's sentence — "in a real recording that happens after a step or two" — is the unstated assumption, and it is the whole question. Students are used to reasoning about the *average* case implicitly and calling it the complexity; this item forces them to notice that they have done so.

Part (c) is where the algorithmic insight has to appear. The nested loop is recomputing something that is already known: the run ending at i is the run ending at i - 1, plus one, whenever the last step is small enough. Recognising that the answer for one input can be read off the answer for the previous one — dynamic programming in its smallest form — turns the quadratic scan into a single pass. The two-line recurrence is easy to write once the observation is made, and almost impossible to reach by optimising the loop.

The classic wrong turns are all present. Measuring on one typical recording and concluding "it is fast"; fixing the performance by adding a break or a cap, which corrupts the longest runs; assuming that abs() or function-call overhead is the bottleneck; and confusing the *amortised* case with the worst case. A further subtlety is worth noting for the strongest answers: the linear algorithm is correct only because the run is defined by *consecutive* differences. If the definition were "all earlier readings within the tolerance of the current reading", a running counter would be wrong, and the fix would be a different data structure. The recurrence is not a trick; it depends on the definition, and saying so is part of understanding why it works.

questions.question:
The finance team has asked you to review the pricing code before the catalogue is extended. The reconciliation compares each customer's stored annual_fee with the invoice total.

(a)

Explain what annual_fee holds for SeatPlan(20, 12) and why it is not equal to monthly_fee() * months. Refer to the order in which the statements in SeatPlan.__init__ and Plan.__init__ run.

[3]

(b)

Construct a corrected design in which the annual fee is always computed from the plan's own seat count and no constructor reads a field of an object that is not yet fully initialised. Use composition: a plan must hold a separate pricing object rather than inherit its price. Write the classes and state the annual fee for 20 seats over 12 months.

[5]

(c)

Calculate the annual fee that every SeatPlan caches, the fee that a 20-seat 12-month plan should be charged, and the total annual shortfall across all 900 customers. State how many of those customers are billed incorrectly.

[4]

(d)

Evaluate the two ways of removing the bug - patching the inheritance hierarchy so the field is set before the superclass constructor runs, or replacing the hierarchy with composition - and recommend one for a catalogue that will soon combine seats, usage and region.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) For SeatPlan(20, 12) the attribute annual_fee holds 108. (A1) It is not 2160 because of the order in which the two constructors run. The first statement of SeatPlan.__init__ is super().__init__(months), and inside Plan.__init__ the assignment self.annual_fee = self.monthly_fee() * months calls self.monthly_fee(). (M1) Because monthly_fee is overridden, that call dispatches to SeatPlan.monthly_fee, which reads self.seats. At that moment the instance has only months in its attribute dictionary - the statement self.seats = seats has not run yet - so the lookup falls back to the class attribute seats = 1. The fee is therefore computed for a one-seat plan: $1 \times 9 = 9$ per month and $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year. (A1) Only after the superclass constructor returns is the instance attribute set to 20, and by then annual_fee has already been stored and is never recomputed; a later call to monthly_fee() correctly returns $20 \times 9 = 180$, so the live query and the cached value disagree.

(b) The defect is not that a constructor calls a method. It is that a constructor calls a method on an object that is only partly built, so the method can observe a field that does not exist yet. Composition removes the half-built object by making the pricing rule a separate, fully constructed collaborator:

class SeatPricing:
    PER_SEAT = 9
    def __init__(self, seats):
        self.seats = seats
    def monthly_fee(self):
        return self.seats * self.PER_SEAT

class Plan:
def __init__(self, months, pricing):
self.months = months
self.pricing = pricing
self.annual_fee = pricing.monthly_fee() * months

p = Plan(12, SeatPricing(20))
print(p.annual_fee) # 2160
```

(M1) for giving Plan a pricing collaborator instead of a subclass that overrides a price method. (A1) for constructing that collaborator completely before the plan uses it, so no method ever reads a field that has not been set. (A1) for computing the annual fee from the collaborator's result. (A1) for the correct value, $180 \times 12 = 2160$. (A1) for noting that Plan.__init__ still calls a method, but on a different object that is already finished, which is why the same line is now safe.

Two inheritance-preserving fixes also work and are acceptable. Assigning the subclass field before the superclass constructor runs:

class SeatPlan(Plan):
    def __init__(self, seats, months):
        self.seats = seats        # set first
        super().__init__(months)  # monthly_fee() now sees 20

and passing the already-computed fee up to the base constructor, so the base never calls an overridable method at all:

class Plan:
    def __init__(self, months, monthly_fee):
        self.months = months
        self.annual_fee = monthly_fee * months

All three produce annual_fee == 2160. (A1)

(c) During construction self.seats always falls back to the class attribute 1, so every SeatPlan caches $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year, whatever its seat count. (M1) At an average of 20 seats the correct fee is $20 \times 9 = 180$ per month, which is $180 \times 12 = 2160$ per year. (A1) The undercharge is therefore $2160 - 108 = 2052$ per customer per year. (A1) Across 900 customers the shortfall is $900 \times 2052 = 1{,}846{,}800$, and all 900 are billed incorrectly: a customer is billed correctly only if it happens to have exactly one seat, which the 20-seat average rules out. The cached fee is one twentieth of the true fee at 20 seats, which is why 108 looks like a plausible annual price for a small team rather than an obvious error. (A1)

(d) Both remedies remove the bug, so the choice is about the next change rather than this one. Patching the hierarchy - assign seats before super().__init__, or pass the fee up - is a one- or two-line change with no runtime cost, but it leaves the base constructor calling an overridable method, so the trap stays armed for the next subclass whose fields are set after super(). (M1) The composition design removes the trap: Plan depends on a SeatPricing object, so a subclass cannot observe an unset field. Its cost is one small object per plan - 900 SeatPricing objects of 48 bytes each, about 309,600 bytes once their instance dictionaries are counted, or roughly 0.31 MB - against a shortfall of 1,846,800. (A1) That is a ratio of about six to one between the money and the memory, so the memory argument is irrelevant at this scale. (A1) The decisive argument is growth: the catalogue will combine seats, usage and region, and inheritance multiplies subclasses (three independent pricing features give up to $2^3 = 8$ subclasses, and each new feature doubles that), while composition adds one collaborator per feature. Recommend adopting composition for the extended catalogue. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question hides a value error inside a language feature that students are taught to admire. Polymorphism is presented as the way a subclass customises behaviour; here it is the mechanism that makes the bug invisible. When Plan.__init__ evaluates self.monthly_fee(), the method that runs belongs to SeatPlan, but the object it runs on is only half built. The field the method needs, seats, does not exist yet, and Python's attribute lookup silently supplies the class attribute instead of raising an error. Nothing crashes, no warning is printed, and the object afterwards looks completely correct: p.seats is 20 and p.monthly_fee() is 180. Only p.annual_fee is wrong, and only for plans whose seat count is not 1.

That last detail is what makes the bug survive testing. The author's tests are not careless - they check that seats are recorded and that the monthly fee scales - but each one either calls the method on demand or uses the single-seat case that the class default happens to match. The failing field is the one computed once, early, and then trusted forever. This is the general shape of a constructor bug: a value is computed at the worst possible moment, cached, and never recomputed, so the error is frozen into the object while every live query returns the truth.

The classic wrong turns are worth naming. The first is to look for the fault in monthly_fee, which is correct. The second is to treat the class attribute seats = 1 as a harmless default and conclude that the value is overwritten before use; it is overwritten, but not before monthly_fee reads it. The third is to fix the symptom by recomputing annual_fee after construction, which hides this instance of the bug while leaving the base constructor's virtual call in place for the next subclass. The fourth, and the most expensive, is to assume that because the object constructs without error the design is sound.

The design lesson is the fragile base class. A superclass that calls an overridable method from its constructor hands every future subclass a hidden ordering constraint that is documented nowhere and enforced by nothing. Composition removes the constraint because the collaborator is finished before it is used: the same line, pricing.monthly_fee() * months, is now safe, which is the point the last part tests. Composition is not free - it costs one object per plan - but at 900 plans the cost is a fraction of a megabyte against a shortfall of nearly two million, so the trade is not close. The remaining judgement is about growth: with three independent pricing dimensions inheritance would need up to eight subclasses, and each new dimension would double that.

questions.question:
The central system must (i) buffer sightings at the gantry, (ii) discard duplicate sightings of the same plate within a 24-hour window, and (iii) merge batches that arrive out of order into one chronological list.

(a)

Explain why a queue is a suitable abstract data type for the gantry's local buffer, and explain one advantage of implementing that queue as a circular queue rather than a non-circular one in this context.

[4]

(b)

Two designs are proposed for discarding duplicates. Design 1 keeps accepted plates in an array and uses linear search. Design 2 keeps accepted plates in a binary search tree keyed on the plate.

For $n$ accepted plates, state the worst-case time complexity of a single membership test for each design, and evaluate which design is preferable for a system handling 40 000 plates per day.

[4]

(c)

Describe, using pseudocode or structured English, an algorithm that merges two batches, each already sorted by timestamp, into a single chronological list. State the time complexity of your algorithm in terms of the batch sizes $p$ and $q$.

[5]

(d)

Number plates are issued in blocks, so plates arriving at a gantry are often already in near-alphabetical order. Explain the consequence of this for the shape and performance of the binary search tree in Design 2, and describe one change that would avoid the problem.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) A queue is suitable because sightings must be removed in the same order in which they arrive: FIFO matches exactly the behaviour of a buffer that is filled by the plate reader and drained by the upload process, whereas a stack would upload the most recent sighting first and destroy the chronological order. (A1)(A1)

The buffer is drained completely every 15 minutes and then refilled, so with a non-circular (linear) queue the front and rear pointers march steadily towards the end of the array; the array appears full even when the queue is nearly empty, and the pointers must be reset or the contents shifted. (M1) In a circular queue the vacated positions at the front are reused as the rear wraps around, so no shifting is needed and the fixed memory allocated to the buffer is used repeatedly — important on an embedded gantry controller with limited RAM. (A1)

(b) Design 1: $O(n)$ — in the worst case (a plate that is not present, or the last element) every one of the $n$ entries must be examined. (A1)

Design 2: $O(\log n)$ for a balanced tree — each comparison halves the remaining search space, so the number of comparisons grows as $\log_{2}n$. (A1)

At 40 000 plates, $\log_{2}(40\,000)\approx15.3$, so Design 2 needs about 15 comparisons per test against up to 40 000 for Design 1 — roughly a factor of 2 600. (M1) Across 40 000 tests per day this is the difference between about $1.6\times10^{9}$ and about $6\times10^{5}$ comparisons per day, so Design 1 is not viable at this volume; Design 2 is clearly preferable. (A1)

(c) Two pointers walk the two batches together, always taking the smaller of the two current timestamps:

MERGE(A, B)                       // A has p items, B has q items, each sorted by timestamp
    i = 0
    j = 0
    C = empty list
    while i < p and j < q         // both batches still have items
        if A[i].timestamp <= B[j].timestamp
            append A[i] to C
            i = i + 1
        else
            append B[j] to C
            j = j + 1
        end if
    end while
    while i < p                   // copy any remainder of A
        append A[i] to C
        i = i + 1
    end while
    while j < q                   // copy any remainder of B
        append B[j] to C
        j = j + 1
    end while
    return C
end MERGE

Award up to (M1) for the two-pointer idea, (A1) for comparing the two current timestamps and appending the smaller, (M1) for terminating when one batch is exhausted, (A1) for correctly copying the remainder of the other batch, and (A1) for stable handling of equal timestamps (using <= rather than <).

Each item is examined and appended exactly once, so the time complexity is $O(p+q)$; the space complexity is also $O(p+q)$ for the merged list. No sorting is required, because both inputs are already sorted.

(d) Inserting keys that are already in order makes every new key the rightmost (or leftmost) node, so the tree never branches: it degenerates into a structure with one node per level — effectively a linked list of height $n$. (A1) The search cost then becomes $O(n)$ rather than $O(\log n)$, so Design 2 loses the entire advantage identified in (b) precisely when the data are easiest to predict. (A1)

One fix: build the tree from the sorted keys by choosing the median as the root and recursing on each half, which produces a balanced tree of height $\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil$. Alternative acceptable fixes: use a self-balancing tree (AVL or red-black) that rebalances on insertion, or shuffle the insertion order. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question looks like an ADT-recall question and is not one. The marking points that separate candidates are all quantitative or conditional:

  • In (b) the phrase 'a binary search tree is faster' is worth nothing on its own; the marks are for turning $\log_{2}(40\,000)\approx15$ into a comparison count and then into a per-day total. Students habitually state complexity classes without evaluating them against a real data volume, which is exactly what the command term asks for here.
  • In (c) the trap is to sort. Both inputs are already sorted, so the merge is linear; a candidate who concatenates and sorts gets the right answer for the wrong reason and at much greater cost. The stability detail (<= rather than <) matters in practice because two gantries can legitimately record the same plate within the same second.
  • In (d) the intended insight is that an ADT's advertised complexity is conditional on an assumption about the data. Keys arriving in sorted order is the canonical case where a binary search tree silently degrades to $O(n)$ — the structure students are taught as 'the efficient one' becomes the worst possible shape. Recognising that complexity claims carry assumptions is the transferable idea.

Classic wrong turns: describing a stack rather than a queue in (a); claiming a circular queue 'has no limit'; and answering (d) with 'use a hash table' without explaining why that helps.

Two further wrong turns recur. In (b) candidates quote the *average* case — 'linear search finds the plate about halfway, so $O(n/2)$' — when the question asks for the worst case; halving $n$ does not change the complexity class, and the two designs stay separated by orders of magnitude. In (c) candidates reach for a sort because 'merging' sounds like 'ordering', when the whole point is that each batch is already ordered: a solution that concatenates and re-sorts has thrown away the only structure the question supplied.

questions.question:
The drone's on-board computer has a general-purpose CPU and a separate GPU.

(a)

Describe how the control unit, the ALU and the registers interact during one fetch–decode–execute cycle.

[4]

(b)

The obstacle-detection workload runs on the GPU rather than the CPU. Explain two architectural differences between a CPU and a GPU and, for each, why it matters for this task. (HL only)

[4]

(c)

The camera produces $1280\times720$ pixel frames at 24 bits per pixel and 30 frames per second.

(i) Calculate the uncompressed data rate in MB per second.

(ii) A codec compresses the video by a factor of 40. Calculate the storage required for a 90-second flight.

[4]

(d)

The flight-control software is written in a high-level language. Evaluate whether it should be compiled or interpreted for the deployed drone. (HL only)

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Award up to four points from:

  • The program counter / control unit holds the address of the next instruction and copies it into the memory address register; the instruction is fetched from memory into the memory data register and then into the instruction register. (A1)
  • The control unit decodes the instruction — determining the opcode and the operands — and sends control signals along the control bus to coordinate the other components. (A1)
  • The ALU performs the actual operation (arithmetic such as adding a sensor offset, or a logical comparison such as testing whether a distance is below a threshold) on data held in registers, setting status/flag bits as a result. (A1)
  • Registers hold the instruction, the operands and the intermediate results, giving much faster access than main memory; the result is written back to a register or to memory and the cycle repeats. (A1)

(b) Award two differences, each with a reason:

| | CPU | GPU | Why it matters here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core design | Few cores, each large, complex and optimised for sequential tasks with heavy branching | Many hundreds or thousands of small, simple cores optimised for throughput | Obstacle detection applies the *same* operation to every pixel; thousands of cores work on different pixels simultaneously |
| Control vs compute | Much of the silicon is devoted to control logic, branch prediction and large caches | Far more of the silicon is devoted to arithmetic units | Image processing is data-parallel with almost no branching, so spending silicon on control logic is wasteful |

Other acceptable differences: SIMD/single-instruction-multiple-data execution; the GPU's higher memory bandwidth; the CPU's higher clock speed and lower latency per task. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)

(c) (i) Bits per frame $=1280\times720\times24=22\,118\,400$ bits (A1)

$$=\frac{22\,118\,400}{8}=2\,764\,800\ \text{bytes}\approx2.76\ \text{MB per frame}$$ (A1)

Data rate $=2.7648\times30=82.9\ \mathrm{MB\,s^{-1}}$ (A1)

(ii) Compressed rate $=\dfrac{82.9}{40}=2.07\ \mathrm{MB\,s^{-1}}$; for 90 s: $2.07\times90=187\ \mathrm{MB}$ (A1)

(Allow 186–188 MB. If 1 MB is taken as $2^{20}$ bytes throughout, the answers are 79.1 MB/s and 178 MB — credit both conventions if used consistently.)

(d) Indicative content:

  • Compiled: translated once into machine code before deployment; execution is fast and predictable because there is no translation at run time; the executable can be optimised for the specific target processor; the source code is not distributed, which protects intellectual property. (A1)(A1)
  • Interpreted: translated line by line at run time; slower (typically by an order of magnitude) and with less predictable timing; but easier to test and modify, and the same source runs on any hardware with a suitable interpreter. (A1)
  • Evaluation: the drone has fixed, known hardware and a hard real-time constraint of 20 ms, and the code will not be modified in flight. Compilation is therefore clearly preferable: the worst-case response time is shorter and, critically, more *predictable* — an interpreter introduces run-time translation delays that could cause a missed deadline and a collision. (A1)

Accept a contrary conclusion only if justified by a specific constraint (for example, if the software had to be updated in flight).

A third option students sometimes offer is just-in-time (JIT) compilation. It should not earn the evaluation mark on its own: a JIT compiler still translates each method at run time the first time it is executed, so the worst-case timing inside a 20 ms control window is not bounded by the source alone, and a routine that runs once per flight never benefits from the cached native code. It earns the same (A1) as any other answer only if the candidate states that the deadline is set by the worst case, and that compilation removes translation from the flight path altogether.
questions.explanation:
Theme A questions are usually pure recall dressed up in a context, and this one is built to resist that. Three things make it harder than it looks:

  • In (a), 'describe the interaction' is not 'list the components'. The fetch–decode–execute cycle is a *sequence* with data moving between named registers, and answers that simply define the control unit, the ALU and the registers separately cannot access the top marks.
  • In (b) the mark scheme is explicitly looking for a difference and a consequence for this workload. 'A GPU has more cores' is a fact; 'obstacle detection applies one operation to every pixel, so thousands of cores each handle a different pixel at the same time' is an explanation.
  • Part (c) is the pivot. Without the number, part (d) is an opinion. With it, students can see that 82.9 MB/s of raw video cannot be stored or processed casually — the compression ratio is doing real work, and any architecture that has to move uncompressed frames around is in trouble.

The evaluation in (d) then has something to bite on. The 20 ms deadline is the decisive constraint: it is not that compilation is 'faster' in some abstract sense, it is that interpretation makes the *worst-case* timing unpredictable, and a hard real-time control loop is governed by its worst case, not its average case.

Classic wrong turns: describing the GPU as 'a faster CPU'; confusing compression ratio with compression *factor* (dividing by 40 when they should, or multiplying); and in (d), describing both options competently and then never choosing.

questions.question:
The network is also used for staff email, VoIP telephony and building-management sensors.

(a)

Calculate the time to transfer one 1.2 GB study over the existing 100 Mbps link. Hence evaluate whether upgrading the link to 1 Gbps would allow the 15-second clinical standard to be met.

[6]

(b)

Explain how packet switching allows the link to be shared with the other traffic listed, and describe one consequence of this sharing for the image transfer.

[4]

(c)

The network is segmented into a clinical VLAN, a guest Wi-Fi VLAN and an IoT VLAN for building sensors. Explain the purpose of this segmentation and how a firewall enforces it.

[3]

(d)

Patient data are encrypted in transit. Distinguish between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, and explain the role of a digital certificate.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) Data: $1.2\ \mathrm{GB}=1.2\times10^{9}\ \text{bytes}=9.6\times10^{9}$ bits. (A1)

Usable bandwidth $=100\times10^{6}\times0.92=92\times10^{6}$ bits per second. (A1)

$$\text{time}=\frac{9.6\times10^{9}}{92\times10^{6}}=104\ \mathrm{s}$$ (A1)

At 1 Gbps: usable $=1000\times10^{6}\times0.92=920\times10^{6}$ bps, so

$$\text{time}=\frac{9.6\times10^{9}}{920\times10^{6}}=10.4\ \mathrm{s}$$ (A1)

Evaluation: the existing link takes about 104 s, roughly seven times the 15 s standard — the requirement is not met and cannot be met by any reasonable tuning. (A1) Upgrading to 1 Gbps gives 10.4 s, which meets the standard but with only about 4.6 s of margin. Since the link is shared with email, VoIP and sensor traffic (see part b), that margin could be eroded at busy times, so a 1 Gbps upgrade is justified but may not on its own be sufficient; the hospital should also consider prioritising (QoS) or transferring studies outside peak hours. (A1)

(b) In a packet-switched network the data is broken into packets, each carrying a destination address and a sequence number. (A1) Packets from different applications are interleaved on the same link, so the link is never idle waiting for one transfer to finish; routers forward each packet independently, possibly by different routes, and the receiving device reassembles them using the sequence numbers. (A1)(A1)

Consequence: the transfer time becomes variable rather than fixed — competing traffic reduces the share of bandwidth available to the image transfer, and because packets may take different routes they can arrive out of order or with varying delay (jitter), so the effective throughput fluctuates and the 104 s figure in (a) is a best case, not a guarantee. (A1)

(c) Segmentation divides one physical network into separate logical networks so that traffic in one segment cannot reach another. (A1) Its purpose here is to contain risk: a compromised guest device or an insecure building sensor cannot reach the clinical network holding patient records, and broadcast traffic is confined. (A1)

A firewall sits between segments and enforces the separation by applying rules — it inspects each packet's source, destination, port and protocol, permits traffic that matches an allowed rule (for example, a clinical workstation on VLAN 10 reaching the image server on TCP port 443) and drops or logs everything else by default. (A1)

(d) Symmetric encryption uses the *same* key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and suitable for bulk data, but the key must be shared securely in advance — if it is intercepted, all communication is compromised. (A1)

Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically related *key pair*: a public key for encrypting and a private key (kept secret) for decrypting. No shared secret needs to be exchanged, but it is far slower, so in practice it is used to exchange a symmetric *session* key, which then encrypts the data. (A1)

A digital certificate solves the remaining problem — how the client knows the public key really belongs to the hospital server and not to an impostor. A trusted certificate authority signs a document binding the server's identity to its public key; the client verifies the signature against the CA's own certificate, and only then uses the public key. (A1)

A self-signed certificate does not solve the problem it appears to. It binds the server's identity to its own key, but the signature is made by the very key being vouched for, so a client that accepts it has no independent evidence of who is at the other end and is open to a man-in-the-middle presenting its own self-signed certificate. Certificates also expire and can be revoked: a client that checks the signature but never checks the validity dates or the revocation information will keep trusting a certificate whose private key has already been compromised.
questions.explanation:
The arithmetic in (a) is easy to get wrong in three specific ways, and each gives an answer that looks plausible: forgetting the 8% overhead (giving 96 s), forgetting that bandwidth is in bits while file size is in bytes (giving 13 s), or applying the overhead by adding rather than multiplying. Only the correct treatment yields 104 s, and without it the evaluation is guesswork.

But the evaluation mark is the real target. '1 Gbps is faster, so upgrade' is not an argument. The student has to notice that 10.4 s leaves under 5 s of headroom on a link that is explicitly shared, and therefore that the upgrade is necessary but possibly not sufficient. That is the difference between describing a network and designing one.

Part (b) is where the two halves of the question connect. The 104 s in (a) is the *unshared* best case. Once packet switching is understood as interleaving rather than queueing, it follows that the real figure will be worse and less predictable — which is exactly why part (a)'s margin matters.

Parts (c) and (d) are deliberately sequenced: segmentation limits *who* can reach the data, and encryption protects it *in transit*. Students commonly conflate the two, or assume that because data are encrypted, network segmentation is unnecessary — it is not, since encryption does nothing to stop an attacker on the clinical VLAN from reaching a server they should not be able to see.

Classic wrong turns: treating 1.2 GB as 1.2 × 2^30 bytes while the question states 10^9; describing circuit switching instead of packet switching; and claiming that a firewall 'encrypts' traffic.

questions.question:
The festival is expanding and the table is causing problems.

(a)

Explain two specific problems with this design, using the data above to illustrate each. For each, name the type of anomaly it represents.

[5]

(b)

Construct a set of tables in third normal form (3NF) to replace PERFORMANCE_BOOKING. State the primary key of each table and show the foreign-key links between them.

[5]

(c)

Using your 3NF design, write an SQL query that lists the customer name, the performance name and the total cost of each booking (quantity × price), for bookings of more than two tickets, ordered by total cost from highest to lowest.

[4]

(d)

Box-office staff need to see booking details but must not see customer email addresses or prices. Explain how a database view solves this. (HL only)

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) Award two from:

  • Update (modification) anomaly. 'Midnight Chorus' and its venue 'East Stage' are repeated in rows 1001, 1002 and 1004. If the performance is moved to another venue, every one of those rows must be changed; if even one is missed, the database holds contradictory answers and a report cannot say where the performance is. (A1)(A1)
  • Insertion anomaly. A newly announced performance cannot be added to the database until someone books it, because the only place a performance name can exist is inside a booking row — and BookingID is the key, so there is no way to store a performance with no bookings. (A1)(A1)
  • Deletion anomaly. If customer L. Oyeka cancels booking 1003, that row is the only record of 'Brass Quartet' at the West Barn; deleting the booking destroys the performance record as well. (A1)(A1)
  • Redundancy / wasted storage. Customer name and email are repeated across every booking that customer makes, so A. Ferrer's details are stored twice and R. Duval's twice, and the repetition grows with the festival. (A1)(A1)

(Maximum 5 marks; at least one answer must name the anomaly type for the higher band.)

(b) A correct 3NF decomposition:

CUSTOMER(CustomerID PK, CustomerName, CustomerEmail)

PERFORMANCE(PerformanceID PK, PerformanceName, VenueName)

SEAT_PRICE(PerformanceID FK, SeatCategory PK *(composite with PerformanceID)*, PricePerTicket)

BOOKING(BookingID PK, CustomerID FK, PerformanceID FK, SeatCategory FK, Quantity)

Award (A1) for separating CUSTOMER, (A1) for separating PERFORMANCE, (A1) for recognising that PricePerTicket depends on the *performance and seat category* pair rather than on the booking (so it needs its own table), (A1) for correct primary keys, (A1) for correct foreign keys linking BOOKING to CUSTOMER and PERFORMANCE.

Why this is 3NF: in every table, each non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. In particular, PricePerTicket is no longer stored against BookingID (a transitive/partial dependency), and VenueName is no longer repeated per booking.

Note: the original table has no CustomerID or PerformanceID, so surrogate keys must be introduced — credit this explicitly if done.

(c) One correct solution:

SELECT c.CustomerName,
       p.PerformanceName,
       b.Quantity * s.PricePerTicket AS TotalCost
FROM BOOKING b
JOIN CUSTOMER    c ON b.CustomerID    = c.CustomerID
JOIN PERFORMANCE p ON b.PerformanceID = p.PerformanceID
JOIN SEAT_PRICE  s ON b.PerformanceID = s.PerformanceID
                  AND b.SeatCategory  = s.SeatCategory
WHERE b.Quantity > 2
ORDER BY TotalCost DESC;

Award (A1) for joining the three or four tables correctly, (A1) for the composite join to SEAT_PRICE (both PerformanceID *and* SeatCategory — joining on SeatCategory alone is the common error and returns wrong prices), (A1) for the computed total and the WHERE b.Quantity > 2 filter, (A1) for ORDER BY TotalCost DESC.

(d) A view is a stored, named query that behaves like a virtual table. (A1) The administrator creates a view exposing only BookingID, CustomerName, PerformanceName, SeatCategory and Quantity, grants box-office staff SELECT on that view, and grants them no privileges at all on the underlying tables. Staff then query the view and cannot reach the excluded columns or the base tables, so security is enforced by the database itself rather than by trusting an application or a member of staff. (A1)

Note for the top band: a view is not a complete security boundary on its own. If the view is updatable, a user granted INSERT or UPDATE on it can change the base tables through the view, so the administrator must grant only SELECT. A user who can see every booking in the view can also infer a customer's identity from a rare performance and a distinctive quantity, so a view controls which columns are visible but not what can be deduced from them. Where the sensitivity lies in the rows rather than the columns, the view must be restricted to a subset of rows as well.
questions.explanation:
Normalisation is one of the topics students can define flawlessly and apply badly. This question is built so that definitions are not enough.

In (a) the anomalies have to be *demonstrated* on the five rows given. 'Repetition causes problems' is not an answer; 'Midnight Chorus is stored three times, so moving it to a different venue means editing three rows, and missing one leaves the database contradicting itself' is. Naming it as an update anomaly is what lifts the answer into the top band.

Part (b) is where the design decisions live, and there are two of them:

1. Customer and performance must be split out — that part is routine.
2. Price is the interesting one. PricePerTicket looks like it belongs to the booking, but it is a property of the (performance, seat category) *pair*: Premium seats for Midnight Chorus cost 85.00 in rows 1001 and 1004, identical because they are the same pair, not because they are the same booking. Leaving price in BOOKING leaves a transitive dependency and the table is not in 3NF. Most candidates miss this.

Part (c) then punishes the mistake automatically: if SEAT_PRICE was not separated out, the query cannot be written correctly, and if it was, the join must be on both PerformanceID and SeatCategory. Joining on SeatCategory alone silently returns several prices per row and a wrong total — the kind of error that produces a plausible-looking report and no error message.

Classic wrong turns: introducing CustomerID but then never using it as a foreign key; writing SELECT with no JOIN conditions (a Cartesian product); and describing a view as a copy of the data (it is not — it is a stored query, and it reflects changes to the base tables immediately).

questions.question:
The bank intends to deploy the model to make automated decisions.

(a)

Distinguish between supervised and unsupervised learning. Identify which type this system uses and justify your answer.

[4]

(b)

For each of the three data issues identified above, describe one appropriate preprocessing step and justify why it is needed. (HL only)

[5]

(c)

The model is trained on 80% of the data and tested on the remaining 20%. Training accuracy is 98% while test accuracy is 71%. Explain what these two figures tell you and what should be done about it. (HL only)

[4]

(d)

After deployment, the model rejects applications from one postcode district at four times the average rate. Discuss two ethical issues this raises and one action the bank should take.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) In supervised learning the training data are *labelled* — each example is paired with the correct output — and the model learns to map inputs to that known target. In unsupervised learning the data are unlabelled and the model must find structure (clusters, associations) on its own. (A1)(A1)

This system is supervised: each of the 40 000 historical applications carries the recorded outcome (repaid or defaulted), which acts as the label, and the task is to predict that outcome for a new applicant. (A1)(A1) (Specifically it is classification, since the output is one of two categories.)

(b)

| Issue | Preprocessing step | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| 12% of income values missing | Impute the missing values — replace them with the median income (or with the median within a relevant subgroup), or drop the rows if 88% is still a large enough sample | Deleting 12% of 40 000 records throws away 4 800 examples and may bias the sample if the missingness is not random; imputing with the *median* rather than the mean avoids distortion by the extreme incomes noted below |
| Income ranges from 0 to 4 000 000 while age ranges 18–75 | Scale / normalise the features — for example min–max scaling to [0, 1] or standardisation (z-scores) | Many algorithms (distance-based methods, gradient descent, regularised models) are dominated by the feature with the largest numeric range; unscaled, income would swamp age and years-in-employment and the model would effectively ignore them |
| Postcode district: 2 800 distinct values | Reduce cardinality — group districts into broader regions, or replace the district with derived features (e.g. average local income from a lookup) rather than using the raw category | 2 800 categories with few examples each makes the model memorise individual districts (overfitting) and makes one-hot encoding produce thousands of sparse columns; it is also the field through which proxy discrimination enters (see part d) |

Award (A1)(A1) for two well-justified steps and (A1) for a third; up to (A1)(A1) overall for the quality of justification. Accept other valid answers: dropping the field entirely, target/mean encoding, or binning income.

(c) The training set is used to fit the model; the test set is data the model has never seen, and it estimates how the model will perform on future applications. (A1)

A training accuracy of 98% with a test accuracy of 71% is a large generalisation gap: the model has fitted the training data extremely closely — including its noise and quirks — but has not learned patterns that transfer. This is overfitting. (A1)(A1)

What to do: reduce model complexity (fewer features or a shallower model), apply regularisation to penalise overly complex fits, gather more training data, use cross-validation to get a more reliable estimate, and — importantly — treat the 71% test figure as the honest estimate of performance rather than the 98%. (A1)

(d) Ethical issues — award two:

  • Indirect (proxy) discrimination. Even if the protected characteristic is not in the dataset, postcode district correlates with ethnic composition, so the model can reproduce discriminatory outcomes while appearing to be neutral. This may be unlawful and is certainly unfair to individual applicants who are judged by their neighbours rather than by their own circumstances. (A1)
  • Lack of transparency / accountability. If the model cannot explain *why* it rejected an application, the bank cannot give a rejected applicant a reason, cannot check whether the decision was lawful, and cannot be held accountable. Automated decisions with significant effects on people require explainability. (A1)
  • Feedback loop. If the model's rejections are fed back into future training data as 'true' outcomes, the bias is reinforced and amplified over time. (A1)
  • Scale of harm. Because decisions are automated, a biased model harms many people consistently and invisibly, rather than as occasional individual lapses. (A1)

Action — award one:
- Audit for disparate impact, test the model's rejection rates across groups, and if the disparity cannot be justified, remove or transform the postcode field and retrain. (A1)
- Keep a human in the loop for borderline or rejected applications, and publish a meaningful reason for each adverse decision. (A1)
- Use fairness-aware techniques: re-weight or re-sample the training data, or constrain the model so that outcomes are independent of the proxy variable. (A1)
questions.explanation:
Machine learning is new enough in the syllabus that most questions about it are definitional. This one is built so that definitions earn the first four marks and the remaining twelve require judgement.

The three data issues in (b) are not arbitrary — each is the classic symptom that has a specific remedy, and the remedy only makes sense once you know what goes wrong without it. Imputation is not about tidiness; it is about not discarding 4 800 examples and not distorting a distribution that has extreme outliers. Scaling is not cosmetic; with income in the millions and age in double digits, an unscaled distance-based or gradient-based model is effectively a model of income alone. Cardinality reduction is not an efficiency trick; 2 800 categories with a handful of examples each guarantees memorisation.

Part (c) is the standard overfitting diagnosis, but the question is phrased so that the student has to say what the *gap* means rather than compute it. The 98%/71% pair is the signature.

The point of the whole question, though, is (d), and it is deliberately connected back to (b). The postcode field is exactly the one whose 'technical' problem — high cardinality — pushes students towards grouping or encoding it, and it is simultaneously the field through which proxy discrimination enters. A student who handles postcode purely as a technical nuisance has missed that the preprocessing decision *is* an ethical decision. That is the transfer this question is trying to test, and it is why the bank's context matters: an unfair loan model does not produce a wrong answer, it produces a life-changing one, automatically, at scale.

Classic wrong turns: calling the system unsupervised because 'the outcome is just recorded'; imputing missing income with 0 (which the model reads as a real value); suggesting more training data as the only cure for overfitting; and proposing 'remove bias from the data' without explaining how bias would be detected.

questions.question:
The 12-bit register stores values in units of 0.0625 degrees Celsius per least significant bit, with the most significant bit carrying the sign.

(a)

Determine the 12-bit two's complement representation of a reading of -37.5 degrees Celsius, giving your answer in binary and in hexadecimal.

[3]

(b)

Explain why the summation register can overflow even when every individual reading is representable, and determine the minimum register width needed to sum any 16 consecutive readings without overflow.

[5]

(c)

Explain why converting a stored reading to degrees Celsius by multiplying by 0.0625 introduces no error, whereas converting it to degrees Fahrenheit does, in both cases assuming the arithmetic itself is performed exactly.

[4]

(d)

Show that F simplifies to P + T.O, and state the number of two-input gates needed for the reduced expression.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) One least significant bit represents $0.0625$ degrees Celsius, so the stored integer is the temperature divided by $0.0625$: $-37.5/0.0625=-600$. (M1)

To store $-600$ in 12-bit two's complement, represent $+600$ first. $600=512+64+16+8$, which is $001001011000$ in 12 bits. (A1)

Inverting every bit gives $110110100111$ and adding 1 gives $110110101000$, so $-600$ is stored as $1101\,1010\,1000$. Grouping into fours from the right: $1101$ is D, $1010$ is A, $1000$ is 8, so the answer is $\mathrm{0xDA8}$. (A1)

*Check: $1101\,1010\,1000$ is $3496$ unsigned, and $3496-4096=-600$. Correct.*

*Representable: $-600$ lies inside the 12-bit signed range $-2048$ to $+2047$, so no clamping is needed.*

(b) A 12-bit two's complement register holds values from $-2048$ to $+2047$. Each individual reading is comfortably inside this range because the largest magnitude the sensor can report is about $128$ degrees Celsius. (M1)

Overflow is a property of the accumulator, not of the sensor. Two readings of $+2047$ already sum to $4094$, which is more than the largest 12-bit signed value, so the sum wraps and a positive result can appear negative. In practice the readings are far smaller than the maximum, but the accumulator has no way of knowing that: it is only 12 bits wide, so any pair of readings above about $1023$ will overflow it. (M1)(A1)

Sixteen readings can each be as large as $2047$, so the largest possible sum is $16\times 2047=32\,752$. (M1) A 15-bit two's complement register reaches only $+16\,383$, which is not enough; a 16-bit register reaches $+32\,767$, which is. The minimum width is therefore 16 bits. (A1)

In general an accumulator summing $k$ readings of width $w$ must satisfy $2^{W-1}-1\ge k(2^{w-1}-1)$; for $w=12$ and $k=16$ the smallest satisfying width is $W=16$, which is why the answer is 16 and not 15.

(c) $0.0625=2^{-4}$. Multiplication by a power of two does not change the digits of a binary number, it only moves the binary point, so the multiplication can be performed by a shift and the result is exact. Every value the sensor can produce is mapped to an exact value in degrees Celsius. (M1)(A1)

The conversion to Fahrenheit is $F=1.8C+32$, so it requires multiplication by $1.8$, which is $9/5$. In binary, $9/5$ is the recurring fraction $1.1100110011\ldots$, which cannot be stored in a fixed number of bits. (M1) Rounding that factor introduces an error that grows with the magnitude of the reading, and because $1/5$ has a factor of 5 in the denominator it can never be represented exactly in binary. (A1)

The Celsius conversion is therefore exact by construction, while the Fahrenheit error is one of representation rather than arithmetic: using more bits shrinks the rounding error but never removes it, because the expansion of $9/5$ does not terminate.

(d) $P.T+P.T'=P.(T+T')=P.1=P$ by the distributive and complement laws. (M1)

Substituting: $F=P+P'.T.O$. (M1)

By the rule $A+A'.B=A+B$ (absorption, or the consensus theorem), with $A=P$ and $B=T.O$, this becomes $F=P+T.O$. (A1)

The reduced expression needs one AND gate for $T.O$ and one OR gate to combine it with $P$, so two two-input gates. (A1) The two inverters required by the original expression are no longer needed, so the gate count falls from five to two and the propagation delay falls as well.

A truth-table cross-check over all eight combinations of $P$, $T$ and $O$ gives identical outputs for the original expression and for $P+T.O$, confirming the simplification.
questions.explanation:
Three separate ideas about fixed-width arithmetic are packed into one device, and they are usually taught separately.

The first is that the representable range depends on the declared width, not on the physical sensor. A 12-bit signed register spans $-2048$ to $+2047$, which comfortably covers a temperature sensor, so a student may reasonably conclude that overflow is impossible. It is not: the accumulator is the same width, and summing is exactly the operation that pushes values out of range. This is why real systems widen the accumulator or use saturating arithmetic, and it is worth knowing that the failure mode of wrapping is silent — a plausible-looking wrong number rather than an error.

The second idea is that exactness in conversion depends on the base representation, not on the size of the number. Multiplying by 0.0625 is exact because it is a power of two. Multiplying by 1.8 is not, and no amount of extra precision fixes it, because 1/5 has no finite binary expansion. This is the same reason that 0.1 cannot be stored exactly as a binary floating-point number, and it is the root cause of a large class of reported bugs in software that handles money.

The third is that a Boolean expression can look as though it needs every term it contains. The term $P.T'$ appears to add information about temperature, but it is redundant: whenever $P$ is true the whole expression is already true, and whenever $P$ is false the term contributes nothing. Recognising this is what the absorption rule formalises. The practical consequence is two gates instead of five, which matters because the alarm output is clocked and every extra gate adds propagation delay.

questions.question:
The four tasks A, B, C and D all become ready simultaneously when the controller wakes. Their processor requirements are 5 ms, 3 ms, 8 ms and 2 ms.

(a)

Describe how a closed-loop control system would maintain soil moisture at a target level, identifying the input, the process, the output and the feedback in your answer.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the average waiting time for the four tasks under first-come-first-served scheduling and under round-robin scheduling with a time quantum of 3 ms, then recalculate each total if every context switch costs 0.5 ms and the tasks are executed in the order A, B, C, D.

[6]

(c)

Explain why the average waiting time alone is a misleading basis for choosing between the two policies, using your figures, and state which policy you would deploy.

[3]

(d)

Evaluate the use of polling for the soil-moisture probe against the use of interrupts for the rain sensor, and explain one additional operating system function that the network connection makes necessary.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) In a closed-loop system the controller measures the actual soil moisture, compares it with the target value, and uses the difference to decide how much water to release; the measurement is then repeated so that the effect of the action is observed and corrected. (M1)

Input: the reading from the soil-moisture probe, converted to a digital value. Process: the controller compares this reading with the target and computes the valve opening and the duration of watering. Output: the signal that opens the irrigation valve, and the water delivered to the plot. Feedback: the next reading from the same probe, which shows whether the moisture has reached the target and allows the next decision to be adjusted. (M1)(A1)(A1)

The feedback path is what makes the system closed-loop and is what distinguishes it from an open-loop system, which would water for a fixed time regardless of the resulting moisture level.

(b) First-come-first-served, executing in the order A, B, C, D:

| Task | Starts | Runs | Completes | Waiting time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 5 | 5 | 0 |
| B | 5 | 3 | 8 | 5 |
| C | 8 | 8 | 16 | 8 |
| D | 16 | 2 | 18 | 16 |

Average waiting time $=(0+5+8+16)/4=7.25$ ms. (M1)(A1)

Round robin with a quantum of 3 ms, queue order A, B, C, D:

| Slice | Task | Runs | Remaining |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A | 3 | 2 |
| 2 | B | 3 | 0 completes at 6 ms |
| 3 | C | 3 | 5 |
| 4 | D | 2 | 0 completes at 11 ms |
| 5 | A | 2 | 0 completes at 13 ms |
| 6 | C | 3 | 2 |
| 7 | C | 2 | 0 completes at 18 ms |

Waiting times are A 8 ms, B 3 ms, C 10 ms and D 9 ms, so the average is $(8+3+10+9)/4=7.50$ ms. (M1)(A1)

Both schedules take 18 ms of processing. First-come-first-served needs 3 context switches, adding 1.5 ms, for a total of 19.5 ms. Round robin needs 7 switches, adding 3.5 ms, for a total of 21.5 ms. (M1)(A1)

(c) Under round robin the average waiting time is 0.25 ms worse and the total time is 2 ms worse, so on the average the two policies are almost indistinguishable and the familiar claim that round robin is fairer is not visible. (M1)

What the average hides is the distribution. Under first-come-first-served the shortest task waits 16 ms, eight times its own running time, and a task that became ready just after a long one would wait longer still. Round robin bounds the wait for any task that is ready: with four tasks and a 3 ms quantum, no task is ever bypassed for more than three slices, so the worst case is 9 ms of other work. (A1)

For a controller whose main job is to keep the valves responding, the bounded worst case is worth more than a marginally better average, so round robin is the defensible choice, with the caveat that the context-switch cost should be reduced before the quantum is made smaller. (A1)

(d) Polling the moisture probe every 30 seconds is cheap and predictable. The probe changes slowly, the event rate is two checks per minute, and the processor overhead of reading a value on a timer is negligible; an interrupt-driven design would add hardware complexity for no benefit. (M1)(A1)

Polling the rain sensor is not acceptable. Drops arrive unpredictably and the required response is within 5 ms, so a polling loop would need a period shorter than 5 ms, consuming processor time continuously and still risking a missed event between samples. An interrupt lets the processor sleep until a drop arrives, which also suits a battery-backed device, and it guarantees the latency requirement rather than merely making it likely. (A1)

The network connection makes authentication and access control necessary: the gateway must be able to accept uploads and possibly commands from the farm network, so the operating system must identify who is allowed to talk to it and protect its memory from a malicious or faulty remote message.
questions.explanation:
The scheduling part of this question is arranged so that the standard intuition fails. Round robin is usually described as fairer, and it is, in the sense that no task is starved. But on this specific workload the average waiting time is very slightly worse and the total time is worse once the context-switch cost is included, because the longest task is interrupted and restarted and the switching overhead is not free. A student who answers 'round robin is fairer' without computing anything has not answered the question, and a student who computes only the averages is forced to choose round robin for a reason the numbers do not support.

The way out is to look at the distribution rather than the mean. Under first-come-first-served the two-millisecond task waits sixteen milliseconds; under round robin nothing waits more than about nine milliseconds. For a device whose purpose is to keep responding to field conditions, the bound matters more than the mean, and that is a genuine engineering judgement rather than a textbook answer.

The second half of the question is about matching a mechanism to an event's statistics. Polling and interrupts are not better or worse in themselves: polling is simpler, has no hardware setup, and is entirely adequate when the event rate is low and the latency requirement is loose, which is exactly the situation of a moisture probe read twice a minute. Interrupts become necessary when the event is rare but must be handled quickly, because a polling loop fast enough to guarantee five-millisecond latency would run continuously and defeat the low-power design. The fact that the two sensors sit on the same device and require opposite answers is the point of the question, and it is the reason a blanket rule such as 'interrupts are more efficient' is unhelpful.

questions.subtopic: A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses (HL only)
questions.question:
The operations director wants the monthly report produced without the dispatch system losing responsiveness. The data described above is available, and management accepts that the reporting and dispatch workloads must be separated.

(a)

Explain why the monthly report is slow and why running it affects the dispatch system, referring to the difference between the workloads the two stores must support.

[4]

(b)

Design a star schema for the monthly report. State the grain of the fact table, name the fact table and three dimension tables, and give two measures that the fact table must hold.

[5]

(c)

Calculate the volume of raw report data generated in one year, and the volume if every record is stored with a replication factor of three. State one consequence of your answer for the choice of database.

[4]

(d)

Justify the use of a key-value or wide-column store for the incoming position reports rather than the relational database, and state one capability that is given up by doing so.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The dispatch system performs online transaction processing: many small reads and writes, each touching a few rows, each required to complete almost immediately. The monthly report performs online analytical processing: it reads almost every row that exists and aggregates it, and it does not care whether the answer arrives in a millisecond. (M1)(A1)

The relational store is organised to make the first workload fast. Its indexes are built on the columns the dispatch system filters on, and those indexes are of no use to a query that must scan the whole of a large table. The monthly report therefore degenerates into a full scan of the position reports, and because the tables are also being written to continuously, the scan has to take locks or work against a moving target. (M1)

Running both workloads on one server means they compete for the same resources: the report's long scan occupies processor time, memory for buffers and disk bandwidth, so the transactional queries queue behind it and the dispatch screen stops responding. This is the standard argument for separating the operational store from a reporting store. (A1)

(b) The grain must be stated before anything else can be decided, because a fact table is only meaningful at one level of detail. Grain: one row per van per completed delivery. (M1)

Fact table: fact_delivery, with one row per delivery and foreign keys to each dimension. (M1)

Dimension tables: dim_date (day, month, year, weekday), dim_depot (depot identifier, depot name, region), and dim_van (van identifier, model, refrigeration capability). A fourth, dim_route, would be defensible if routes are named rather than being defined by origin and destination, and should be accepted. (M1)

Measures: at least two numeric, additive quantities such as delivery_duration_minutes and distance_km, together with temperature_excursions, which is stored as a count of qualifying events rather than as a duration so that it can be summed. (M1)(A1)

Storing the delivery duration as a measure rather than deriving it from timestamps is what makes the average delivery time per depot obtainable without touching the raw reports at all.

(c) 340 vans write one report every 0.4 seconds for 14 hours a day: each van produces $14\times 3600/0.4=126\,000$ reports per day, so the fleet produces $340\times 126\,000=42\,840\,000$ reports per day. (M1)

At 80 bytes each, that is $42\,840\,000\times 80=3.43\times 10^{9}$ bytes, which is 3.43 GB per day. (A1)

Over 365 days the raw volume is $3.43\times 365=1\,251$ GB, approximately 1.25 TB per year. (A1) With a replication factor of three the stored volume is about 3.75 TB. (A1)

One consequence follows directly: a single relational server cannot be the store for this data, because the write rate alone is over a million rows per minute across the fleet at peak and the table grows by terabytes annually. A distributed store that partitions the data across nodes is required, and retention policy becomes a design decision rather than an afterthought.

(d) The incoming reports have a very simple shape and an extremely high write rate, and the query pattern is almost always 'give me the reports for this van between these two times'. (M1) A key-value or wide-column store matches this exactly: the key is the van identifier combined with the timestamp, writes are append-only and can be spread across nodes, and a time-range read is a contiguous scan within one partition. No joins are required, so the relational model's main advantage is not being used.

The capability given up is transactional consistency across records: ACID guarantees are weakened in exchange for availability and partition tolerance, so a system reading the store may see data that is not yet complete or not yet consistent everywhere. (A1)(A1) For position reports this is acceptable; for the financial records of the same company it would not be, which is why the two stores coexist rather than one replacing the other.
questions.explanation:
The question turns on a distinction that is easy to state and hard to apply: the same data can require two different storage systems because the two workloads have opposite shapes. The dispatch system does many small operations that must each finish quickly; the monthly report does one enormous aggregation that nobody minds waiting for. A schema optimised for the first is actively hostile to the second, because the indexes that make row lookups fast are irrelevant to a full scan, and because the scan competes for resources with the transactions.

Part (b) is the part most likely to be attempted without the necessary discipline. A star schema is defined by its grain, and the grain must be the finest thing the measures are meaningful at. Writing 'per depot per month' produces a table that already contains the answer and cannot be re-aggregated differently, which defeats the purpose of a warehouse. Stating the grain as one row per van per completed delivery keeps the table re-aggregatable by any dimension, and that is precisely the flexibility a warehouse is bought for. The dimension tables exist so that the query can group by month, depot or van without a join to the operational database.

Part (c) is arithmetic with a design consequence. Roughly 43 million reports a day at 80 bytes gives about 3.4 GB daily and about 1.25 TB a year before replication; the moment a replication factor is added, the figure is well beyond what a single server should hold. The useful observation is not the number itself but what it rules out: the storage decision is forced by the write rate, not by a preference for novel technology.

Part (d) closes the argument. A time-series access pattern with no joins is exactly what a key-value or wide-column store is good at, and choosing it costs the transactional guarantees that the financial system still needs. Both stores therefore exist, and the fact that they hold overlapping data is a deliberate redundancy rather than a design failure.

questions.question:
The window size is a property of the device, not of any individual object, and several SensorReadings objects may exist at once for different sensors.

(a)

Explain why CAPACITY should be a class-level constant rather than an instance variable set by __init__, and state one invariant that the class must maintain.

[3]

(b)

Construct the completed class, including __init__, add, mean and __len__, so that it maintains the invariant you stated and never holds more than CAPACITY readings.

[6]

(c)

Explain the error in the draft mean method and the effect it has after three readings have been added to a buffer whose capacity is five, and state the corrected line.

[4]

(d)

Explain why a method that returns self.values directly breaks encapsulation, and describe one way of giving the caller the data without doing so.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The window size is a property of the device, is the same for every object created, and must not vary between objects; making it a class-level constant expresses that and prevents one instance from being given a different capacity from another. (M1) It also removes the risk that the value is reassigned after construction, which would make the buffer's behaviour depend on when a method was called. (A1)

An invariant the class must maintain: the number of readings held is never greater than CAPACITY, and the values held are always the most recent ones added, in order. (A1)

(b)

class SensorReadings:
    CAPACITY = 5

def __init__(self):
self._values = []

def add(self, reading):
if len(self._values) == self.CAPACITY:
self._values.pop(0)
self._values.append(reading)

def mean(self):
if not self._values:
return None
return sum(self._values) / len(self._values)

def __len__(self):
return len(self._values)
```

The critical construction is the eviction in add: the oldest reading is removed before the new one is appended, which is what keeps the length bounded. (M1)(A1) The guard inside mean handles the empty buffer, which would otherwise raise a division by zero; the guard must be present because the class is usable before any reading arrives. (M1)(A1)

Using len(self._values) rather than a stored count means the count cannot fall out of step with the list. (M1) The attributes are prefixed with a single underscore to signal that they are internal, and __len__ gives callers the size without exposing the list. (A1)

(c) The error is that mean divides the total by self.capacity, the maximum number of readings the buffer can hold, instead of by the number of readings it actually holds. (M1)

With a capacity of five and three readings added, say 10, 20 and 30, the total is 60 and the correct mean is $60/3=20$. The draft returns $60/5=12$. (M1)(A1) The error is therefore not a failure but an understatement: the displayed average is too low by a factor of 3/5, and because the divisor is fixed, the error shrinks as the buffer fills and disappears entirely once five readings have been added. That is why testing with a single reading and then a few more gives values that look plausible. (A1)

The corrected line is:

        return total / len(self.values)

The same correction is what makes the earlier version of mean safe against an empty buffer, since a division of zero by zero would otherwise raise an exception.

(d) Returning self.values hands the caller a reference to the internal list, not a copy. (M1) The caller can then append to it, sort it in place or clear it, and every one of those operations changes the state of the object without going through add, which is the only method that enforces the capacity limit. The invariant established in part (b) is then broken from outside the class, and the object can end up holding more readings than CAPACITY or in an order that no longer reflects when they arrived. (A1)

One way to avoid this is to return a copy of the list, for example return list(self._values), so that the caller's changes affect only their own copy. (A1) A generator that yields each reading in turn achieves the same protection while avoiding the cost of copying a large buffer.

Note that list(self._values) is a shallow copy: it protects the list itself, but if the readings were mutable objects rather than numbers the caller would still share the same objects and could mutate them in place. For numeric readings the distinction does not bite, which is why the question uses temperatures; a class holding mutable records would need a deep copy, or better, to hand back immutable values.
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a bug that a cursory test will not find. When only one reading has been added, the draft's mean divides by the capacity and returns a number that is wrong but not obviously so; as more readings arrive the divisor becomes closer to the truth, and once the buffer is full the bug disappears entirely. A student who tests with a full buffer will conclude that the class works. That is exactly the failure mode of real code that maintains a rolling statistic, and it is why the question asks for the effect after three readings out of five rather than at the end.

The design issue underneath is the difference between the capacity and the count. They are equal only when the buffer is full, and code that uses them interchangeably is correct in the case people test and wrong in the case that matters. Writing the class so that the count is always derived from the data, rather than stored separately, removes the possibility of the two drifting apart — a small decision with a large effect on how many bugs the class can have.

The encapsulation part is not a formality. Returning the internal list gives the caller a reference, and the caller can then violate the invariant that add was written to protect. This is the most common way that a class with a carefully written interface is broken from the outside, and the fix is not to document the danger but to remove it by returning a copy or yielding values. The same reasoning explains why the attributes are private: the capacity rule lives in add, and nothing should be able to bypass it.

Finally, making the capacity a class-level constant expresses something true about the problem — the window size belongs to the device, not to an individual window object — and it makes the invariant checkable, since a value that cannot be reassigned per object cannot be violated per object.
